title: The Promotion

jokes.text: Michael declares expense reports are 'a day-to-day item' and that he is exclusively 'big picture, epic, Gone with the Wind.'
jokes.setup: An employee asks Michael to sign an expense report, a mundane managerial task.
jokes.punchline: Michael refuses by invoking 'Gone with the Wind' as his governing philosophy of leadership.
jokes.explanation: Classic Michael Scott delusion — he genuinely believes his role has elevated him beyond paperwork. The 'Gone with the Wind' reference is perfectly absurd and character-specific. Sets up the entire episode's conflict efficiently.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Gone with the Wind.' Employee: 'Never saw it.' Michael: 'Me neither. Chick flick.'
jokes.setup: Michael name-drops Gone with the Wind as his aspirational leadership model.
jokes.punchline: Neither he nor the employee has seen it — and Michael immediately dismisses it as a chick flick, undermining his own grandiose reference.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy — in three short lines, Michael's pomposity is completely deflated by his own ignorance. The rapid-fire 'Me neither. Chick flick.' is perfectly timed self-own that only works because Michael has zero self-awareness. The two-beat structure is airtight. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in its sharpness and economy.

jokes.text: Employee asks to be 'grandfathered in' on Michael signing expense reports. Michael is baffled. Employee explains it means Michael would still do what he used to do. Michael: 'That doesn't make any sense because I would still be doing exactly what I used to do.'
jokes.setup: Employee uses 'grandfathered in' as a logical workaround to get Michael to keep doing his old duties.
jokes.punchline: Michael correctly identifies the logical flaw but from a position of total confusion, revealing he doesn't understand the concept at all while accidentally being right.
jokes.explanation: A solid joke about Michael accidentally being correct for the wrong reasons. The confusion is authentic to his character but the execution is a bit slow. Functional.

jokes.text: Michael to employee: 'You're making my brain smaller. Get out.'
jokes.setup: Employee attempts to reason with Michael about the grandfathering concept.
jokes.punchline: Michael dismisses him with the medically absurd claim that the conversation is physically shrinking his brain.
jokes.explanation: Quotable and efficient. 'You're making my brain smaller' is a great Michael Scott non sequitur that perfectly captures his defensive illogic. Strong economy.

jokes.text: Employee responds to 'You're making my brain smaller' with a story about his uncle who went mad and had to be buried, only for Michael to say 'I am so sick of that story. Get out.'
jokes.setup: The employee seems to be starting a sympathetic story about someone whose brain got smaller — validating Michael's absurd claim.
jokes.punchline: The story escalates to the uncle being starved, going mad, and being buried — and Michael cuts it off saying he's heard it too many times, implying this insane story is a regular occurrence in their interactions.
jokes.explanation: The dark escalation (starved, went mad, buried) followed by Michael's weary 'I am so sick of that story' is wonderfully absurd. The punchline reframes the employee as someone with a genuinely unhinged family history that Michael has simply grown tired of hearing. Solid misdirection.

jokes.text: Dwight approaches Jim with an expense report. Jim says 'Where's the please? We're not animals.' Dwight refuses to say please. Jim refuses to sign without it.
jokes.setup: Dwight needs Jim to sign his expense report and simply says 'Sign this.'
jokes.punchline: Jim, now in a small position of authority, exerts it on the petty level of demanding 'please' — and neither man will yield, reducing management to a playground standoff.
jokes.explanation: Works because it perfectly captures the Jim/Dwight dynamic — Jim is using his new tiny authority to torment Dwight in the most juvenile way possible. 'We're not animals' is a good line. Efficient and character-specific.

jokes.text: Dwight walks away from Jim muttering 'Idiot' to camera.
jokes.setup: Jim refuses to sign without a 'please' and Dwight refuses to say it.
jokes.punchline: Dwight breaks away and delivers a single disgusted word directly: 'Idiot.' The camera beat undercuts both of them — Dwight is the one who lost the standoff.
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy — one word does all the work. Dwight calling Jim an idiot while being the one who refused to say 'please' like an adult is self-undermining in classic Dwight fashion.

jokes.text: Dwight goes to Michael to complain about Jim, framing it as a 'huge, enormous, massive complaint about the tallest guy in our office.'
jokes.setup: Dwight wants Michael to intervene in his expense report dispute with Jim.
jokes.punchline: He describes it as 'big picture' to satisfy Michael's new framework, using grandiose language ('huge, enormous, massive') to dress up an utterly petty grievance, and describes Jim only as 'the tallest guy in our office.'
jokes.explanation: Dwight adapting Michael's own 'big picture' language to sneak a petty complaint past him is good character work. 'The tallest guy in our office' as a Dwight descriptor for Jim has a fun childishness to it.

jokes.text: Jim takes Dwight's complaint about Jim himself, asks who it's about, and when Dwight says 'You!', Jim responds 'Okay. Just want to let you know I take complaints very seriously. So...when did this happen?'
jokes.setup: Dwight goes to Jim to complain about Jim.
jokes.punchline: Jim, perfectly deadpan, proceeds to formally process the complaint against himself, including asking Dwight how he feels and whether he cried.
jokes.explanation: This is a great Jim bit — using his new managerial bureaucracy as a weapon against Dwight while maintaining complete sincerity. The escalation into asking 'Did he hit you? Did you cry? Did you feel like crying?' makes it better with each beat. Exceptional character integration: only Jim would think to do this, and only Dwight would go along with it long enough to get trapped.

jokes.text: Jim writes 'held back tears' in the complaint report after Dwight says no to everything. Dwight: 'Wait, stop writing that. That is not true.' Jim: 'If you stop crying, I'll stop writing it.' Dwight: 'I'm not cr-- uhh!'
jokes.setup: Jim is formally processing Dwight's complaint and asks if he cried or felt like crying — Dwight says no to all.
jokes.punchline: Jim writes 'held back tears' anyway, then traps Dwight in a catch-22: 'If you stop crying, I'll stop writing it.' Dwight's exasperated 'I'm not cr-- uhh!' is the perfect losing reaction.
jokes.explanation: This is the standout joke of the opening sequence. The 'If you stop crying, I'll stop writing it' line is a masterpiece of Jim's torment — it's a logical Möbius strip that traps Dwight perfectly. The structure is immaculate: setup the question, deny the answer, create the paradox, get the reaction. Dwight's cut-off 'I'm not cr-- uhh!' sells the complete defeat. This is premium Office comedy writing that approaches the 8.0 anchor caliber.

jokes.text: Dwight's complaint fantasy escalates into a full wrestling match description: triangle choke hold, hammer lock, 'he's gasping, he's panting. Every last breath. And the crowd is going crazy. And boom! I emerge victorious! $18,000 and a chance at the title!'
jokes.setup: Dwight says his demotion makes him want to put Jim in a 'triangle choke hold.'
jokes.punchline: The fantasy rapidly escalates through professional wrestling moves to a full championship bout with prize money and a title shot — Dwight delivering it with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: The escalation structure is well-done — each beat raises the absurdity. '$18,000 and a chance at the title' is the perfect peak. Fully in character for Dwight, who would absolutely narrate his own fantasy victory. The 'Ooh hah!' celebration caps it nicely.

jokes.text: Dwight delivers the punchline to his entire wrestling fantasy: 'Jim wants you to keep it down.'
jokes.setup: Dwight has been delivering a passionate, full-body wrestling fantasy about defeating Jim.
jokes.punchline: The scene cuts to an employee delivering a mundane message from Jim asking Dwight to be quieter — Jim's authority literally interrupting and deflating Dwight's rebellion fantasy.
jokes.explanation: Structurally superb — the scene timing and punchline deflation is near-perfect. After Dwight's epic self-aggrandizing fantasy, Jim is so unbothered he just sends someone to tell Dwight to pipe down. The authority relationship is perfectly summarized in a single line. The economy of '...Jim wants you to keep it down' after 45 seconds of escalating fantasy is exceptional craft.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Go ahead, name a country that doesn't have two presidents. A boat that sets sail without two captains. Where would Catholicism be without the popes?'
jokes.setup: Michael is defending the idea that two leaders is obviously better.
jokes.punchline: He lists examples of shared leadership — all of which are either completely false (countries have one president, boats have one captain) or accidentally grammatically wrong ('the popes' implies multiple popes simultaneously).
jokes.explanation: One of the best Michael Scott lines in the episode. The list structure is perfect — each example is more wrong than the last, building to 'Where would Catholicism be without the popes?' which is both grammatically bizarre and theologically confused. The confident rhetorical question format ('Go ahead, name a country...') makes Michael's ignorance even funnier. Highly quotable, fully character-integrated. Approaches the 8.0 anchor benchmark.

jokes.text: Michael traces a line from toilet paper to human anatomy to outer space planets in a conference room meeting justification.
jokes.setup: Jim challenges Michael about excessive conference room meetings, citing 'a meeting about planets.'
jokes.punchline: Michael explains the meeting started about toilet paper, moved to which body part uses it, and then 'you draw a line from there to the other planets' — presented as a perfectly logical educational journey.
jokes.explanation: The comedic journey from toilet paper → buttocks → planets is absurdist gold. Michael's sincere conclusion that 'by the end, we all learned a little bit about how small we are' gives the joke a philosophical veneer that makes it even funnier. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Michael explains that a meeting about planets started as a toilet paper discussion: 'What part of the human body does one use toilet paper upon? So you draw a line from there to the other planets.'
jokes.setup: Jim asks Michael about having a meeting about planets, suggesting it's a waste of time.
jokes.punchline: Michael explains the meeting's logic: toilet paper → the body part you use it on → by extension, planets. It's a completely incoherent through-line delivered as reasonable narrative.
jokes.explanation: The logical leaps are absurd but Michael treats the reasoning as self-evident, which is perfect character comedy. 'You draw a line from there to the other planets' is genuinely funny. The philosophical coda ('we all learned a little bit about how small we are... it's a big universe') makes it even better by suggesting the meeting ended on a sincere note of cosmic wonder.

jokes.text: Michael: 'You know what eats a large amount of the day are naps. You go to sleep, it's light out, you wake up, it's dark. That's the whole day. Where did that day go? I have no idea.'
jokes.setup: Jim says that Michael's frequent meetings 'eat large amounts of the day.'
jokes.punchline: Michael redirects to naps as the real time-eater, delivering a genuine philosophical bafflement about falling asleep during the day — implying he regularly naps at work and doesn't know where weekdays go.
jokes.explanation: Michael napping at work and being genuinely mystified by where the day went is quietly brilliant. The deadpan 'I have no idea' suggests he's had this experience multiple times. Jim's correction 'You mean on a weekend' and Michael's immediate 'Yes' is a perfect button.

jokes.text: Jim: 'You mean on a weekend.' Michael: 'Yes.'
jokes.setup: Michael describes napping through entire days as a relatable experience.
jokes.punchline: Jim gently suggests he means on weekends. Michael immediately agrees — but the agreement itself is a lie, since he clearly naps at work.
jokes.explanation: A clean button on joke #16. Jim's one-line course-correction and Michael's instant capitulation efficiently close the bit. Strong economy.

jokes.text: Jim's talking-head confessional: 'Oh, sure — things are great. For Michael. Absolutely nothing's changed for him...But today, Jim Halpert puts his foot down.' Cut to: 'So that was three days ago, and it didn't take. But today, mark my words, Jim Halpert really, really puts his foot down.'
jokes.setup: Jim declares with conviction that he's putting his foot down with Michael.
jokes.punchline: Immediate cut revealing that declaration was three days ago and nothing changed — then Jim makes the same declaration again, more emphatically, undermining himself further.
jokes.explanation: The mockumentary structure is used masterfully here — the time-jump punchline ('that was three days ago, and it didn't take') completely deflates Jim's declaration, then the immediate re-declaration ('really, really puts his foot down') doubles the comedy. This is how the show's format can generate jokes unavailable to any other structure. Strong craft.

jokes.text: Pam tells someone she needs to fit into her wedding dress. Beat. 'However, I'm also pregnant.'
jokes.setup: Pam explains she's watching what she eats because she needs to fit into her wedding dress — a relatable, conventional concern.
jokes.punchline: After a pause, she adds 'However, I'm also pregnant' — revealing the complication that makes the wedding dress concern absurdist.
jokes.explanation: The pause between the normal statement and 'However, I'm also pregnant' is the whole joke — 'however' is an unusually formal conjunction that creates great comic distance. The delivery is perfectly Pam: understated and matter-of-fact. The structure is very clean.

jokes.text: Someone tells Pam: 'It's a myth that women have to gain more than nine pounds in a pregnancy? Look at these actresses. Some of them lose weight.'
jokes.setup: Pam has revealed she's pregnant and trying to fit into her wedding dress.
jokes.punchline: An office worker responds with medically dubious advice about pregnancy weight gain, framed around celebrity gossip, delivered with total confidence.
jokes.explanation: Competent cringe — someone giving Pam terrible unsolicited pregnancy advice. Works as a standard Office awkward-coworker beat but doesn't rise above functional. Character identity unclear reduces the impact.

jokes.text: Pam on registering for gifts: 'We did, but mostly because people expect us to.' Pause. 'We're also accepting other gifts not on the registry.' Pause. 'However much. It's awkward asking people for money, but we could really use it. Why doesn't Crate & Barrel let you register for a toaster full of cash?'
jokes.setup: Someone asks about the wedding registry.
jokes.punchline: Pam's answer escalates from politely conventional ('mostly because people expect us to') to nakedly mercenary ('however much') to a genuinely inspired product idea: 'a toaster full of cash.'
jokes.explanation: 'A toaster full of cash' is genuinely quotable and a funny specific image. The escalating honesty of Pam's gift-begging is well-structured — she peels back social niceties one layer at a time. 'However much' delivered as a casual afterthought is the best beat.

jokes.text: Phyllis tells Pam that her cousin makes 'the most amazing romantic birdhouse mailboxes' and that Pam will 'still be surprised when you see it' — then asks 'You're not registered for a birdhouse, are you?' Pam: 'No, we're not.' Phyllis: 'Good. Good.'
jokes.setup: Pam has explained they want cash gifts.
jokes.punchline: Phyllis has already clearly decided to give them a birdhouse mailbox and is seeking confirmation it won't conflict with a registry — the attempt to claim Pam will 'still be surprised' while describing the exact gift is oblivious social comedy.
jokes.explanation: Classic Office oblivious coworker moment. Phyllis completely ignoring Pam's 'we want cash' to check if her pre-planned birdhouse gift is acceptable is perfectly in character. 'Good. Good.' as a button is solid.

jokes.text: Someone eating loudly at their desk ('Mmm. Mmm. Mmm.'). Another employee says 'Do you mind?' The eater responds: 'I'll tell you what. You show me one of those crossword puzzles that you've finished and I'll be quieter.'
jokes.setup: An employee is eating loudly and disturbing a coworker who does crossword puzzles.
jokes.punchline: The eater retaliates by demanding proof of the crossword-doer's intellectual legitimacy before offering to be quiet — a completely unrelated and irrational negotiating position.
jokes.explanation: The counterattack logic is absurd and funny — 'prove you can do crosswords and then I'll eat quieter' makes zero sense but is delivered as a completely reasonable position. Good wordless comedy in the setup (the Mmm sounds) followed by a sharp retort.

jokes.text: Employees discover Jim's memo requiring 20 cold calls a day. One says: 'I hate making cold calls. It's like trying to sleep with someone you've only known for a month — it's impossible.'
jokes.setup: Employees are upset about Jim's new cold-calling policy.
jokes.punchline: The analogy comparing cold calls to sleeping with a month-long acquaintance is presented as making sense — and then declared 'impossible,' which is more revealing about the speaker's personal life than their professional objections.
jokes.explanation: A solid observational joke with a nice secondary layer — the 'it's impossible' implies a pretty conservative personal life. Works as character comedy even without knowing exactly who says it.

jokes.text: After the cold calls complaint, another employee adds: 'And get a new haircut.' First employee: 'Thank you, I've been saying that for years.'
jokes.setup: Employees are listing grievances about Jim as manager.
jokes.punchline: One employee adds Jim's haircut as a legitimate workplace complaint — and the other has apparently been nursing this grievance for years.
jokes.explanation: A quick, effective joke about the pettiness of office grievances. 'I've been saying that for years' suggests a years-long silent campaign against Jim's hair. Light but functional.

jokes.text: Dwight in talking head: 'If the people here were our founding fathers, the Revolutionary War would have been delayed ten years because Stanley Washington was napping, and Phyllis Hancock was still signing the Declaration, and Kevin Jefferson was distracted by a butterfly.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is expressing hope that his coworkers will rise up and revolt against Jim's management.
jokes.punchline: He assigns each coworker a founding father persona that perfectly maps to their Office character flaws — Stanley=lazy, Phyllis=slow, Kevin=distracted — in an elaborate historical analogy.
jokes.explanation: This is an exceptional Dwight joke — his grandiosity combined with accurate character observation creates something greater than the sum of its parts. 'Kevin Jefferson was distracted by a butterfly' is the perfect escalating button. The historical framing is exactly what Dwight would do: invoke the Founding Fathers to complain about coworkers. The name pairings are clever. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Dwight's talking head: 'Big Tuna is starting to stink a little... People are starting to notice how terrible Jim is. It's great. Eventually, they'll rise up and revolt.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is commenting on growing resentment toward Jim among coworkers.
jokes.punchline: Dwight frames ordinary workplace griping as the preconditions for revolutionary uprising — with sincere glee.
jokes.explanation: Dwight's revolutionary rhetoric applied to office politics is consistently funny. His sincerity about the 'revolt' is what makes it work. 'Big Tuna is starting to stink' is a nice double meaning (Jim's nickname vs. a fish metaphor).

jokes.text: An employee congratulates Jim on his promotion, then asks him to 'forget what I said last week...about the fact that I don't really do my job.'
jokes.setup: An employee approaches Jim seemingly to congratulate him.
jokes.punchline: The congratulations are a cover to ask Jim to forget an apparently self-incriminating confession about not doing his job — the employee has been avoiding Jim for a week over this.
jokes.explanation: Solid cringe setup — the employee's nervous revelation compounds itself. Works as an efficient character moment showing how Jim's promotion has changed the office dynamic.

jokes.text: Jim tells the employee he should probably stop telling Jim these things. Employee: 'Gotcha.' Then immediately adds: 'It was just that I was late today and I took a nap in the bathroom for a while.'
jokes.setup: Jim advises the employee to stop confessing self-incriminating information to his new manager.
jokes.punchline: The employee agrees ('Gotcha') and then immediately continues confessing — revealing he napped in the bathroom today.
jokes.explanation: The callback escalation is perfectly timed — 'Gotcha' followed by immediate failure is a reliable comedy structure, but the specificity of 'nap in the bathroom' makes it memorable. Jim's 'Mm-hmm?' after is a great reaction beat.

jokes.text: Jim walks in on Michael's secret 'focus group' meeting. Jim: 'Hey, Stanley, what was the last thing Michael said before I came through the door?' Stanley: 'If you don't smell this, you're fired.'
jokes.setup: Jim catches Michael holding an unauthorized conference room meeting disguised as a 'focus group.'
jokes.punchline: Stanley reveals the last thing Michael said was 'If you don't smell this, you're fired' — confirming the meeting was completely unproductive and possibly bizarre, while also showing Stanley will casually throw Michael under the bus.
jokes.explanation: 'If you don't smell this, you're fired' is a perfect Michael Scott non sequitur that tells us everything about his management style in one line. Stanley's willingness to immediately betray Michael is also perfectly in character. Jim's use of Stanley as a witness against Michael is a smart comedic move.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Listen, Jim, no offense, but when push comes to shove, what I want is more important than what you want.' Then turns to the focus group: 'What do you guys think?'
jokes.setup: Jim tells Michael this isn't a conference room meeting and asserts co-manager authority.
jokes.punchline: Michael makes an authoritarian statement about his wants mattering more, then immediately undermines it by polling the room — demonstrating he needs external validation even for his power assertions.
jokes.explanation: The pivot to 'What do you guys think?' after asserting dominance is a perfect Michael self-undermining. He can't even claim authority without needing people to agree. Solid character work.

jokes.text: Talking head comparison of Jim vs. Michael: 'Comparing Jim and Michael is like comparing apples and oranges. I like apples, and I really, really don't like oranges. Oranges are annoying and hate me.'
jokes.setup: Employee uses the 'apples and oranges' idiom to compare the two managers.
jokes.punchline: The metaphor breaks down immediately into a personal feud with oranges — 'Oranges are annoying and hate me' — which reveals more about the speaker's psychology than the managers.
jokes.explanation: 'Oranges are annoying and hate me' is a genuinely funny escalation from a stock idiom. The character commits fully to the fruit metaphor in a way that becomes inadvertently revealing. Good joke structure.

jokes.text: Talking head: 'When you ask Jim a question, he'll tell you the answer. When you ask Michael a question, he'll do an imitation of you for five minutes and then when that doesn't work, he'll try to tickle you. But he also doesn't care if you come in late, so I guess I prefer Michael.'
jokes.setup: Employee is comparing Jim and Michael as managers.
jokes.punchline: The damning indictment of Michael ('imitation... then tickle you') is immediately overridden by the punchline: Michael's incompetence is preferable because of the attendance policy.
jokes.explanation: Excellent structure — builds a devastating case against Michael ('imitation for five minutes, then try to tickle you') and then undercuts it entirely with an extremely low-bar preference. 'I guess I prefer Michael' as a conclusion after describing his management as tickling-based is a great payoff. The 'imitate you for five minutes then tickle' description of Michael is also a genuinely precise and funny observation.

jokes.text: Andy's talking head: 'Michael is like the fun dad. Jim is like the serious mom. And wittle Andy is stuck in the middle, and he wuvs them both vewy much, but if he had to pick one, well, goodness gracious, he would probably pick Jim because Jim gives Andy his num-nums on time. Num-nums are, of course, my commission checks.'
jokes.setup: Andy is asked to compare the two managers.
jokes.punchline: Andy describes the management situation as a family drama — with himself as a baby — then snaps back to adult business language for the explanation of 'num-nums.'
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best talking heads. The baby-talk escalation ('wittle Andy,' 'wuvs,' 'vewy much,' 'num-nums') is perfectly committed and then the snap back to 'Num-nums are, of course, my commission checks' is a perfect joke construction. Only Andy Bernard could deliver this — his fragile emotional regression is totally in character. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Talking head: 'I love rivalries — Michael or Jim, Paris or Nicole, Heidi or L.C. ...I'd have to go with L.C. Heidi's a bad friend, and her skin is terrible.'
jokes.setup: Employee is asked to weigh in on the Michael vs. Jim rivalry.
jokes.punchline: After mentioning Paris/Nicole and Heidi/L.C. from The Hills, the employee abandons the original question entirely to give a decisive verdict on the Heidi/L.C. feud, with specific criticism of Heidi's skin.
jokes.explanation: A solid non sequitur — pivoting from a workplace management question to a decisive reality-TV verdict. 'Her skin is terrible' as a concluding judgment is funny. Ages slightly due to the Hills reference but was well-timed for 2009.

jokes.text: David Wallace calls the office at exactly the moment Jim and Michael were debating whether to call him. 'Or David Wallace will call us on line two.'
jokes.setup: Jim suggests they call David Wallace to resolve their dispute. Michael insists HE will be the one to call David Wallace.
jokes.punchline: David Wallace calls them first, undermining the entire argument about who calls whom.
jokes.explanation: Good structural comedy — the argument about who gets to call Wallace is immediately made irrelevant by Wallace calling them. The timing lands well. Michael's 'Why don't we just—' getting interrupted by the actual call is a solid beat.

jokes.text: During the Wallace call, Jim reveals Michael has been texting Wallace during the conversation. 'Wait, I'm sorry. Michael, are you— are you texting me?' Michael: 'I thought maybe we could talk after this is over.'
jokes.setup: Michael is on a group call with Jim and David Wallace about a serious business matter.
jokes.punchline: Michael has been simultaneously texting Wallace for a side conversation — like a kid passing notes in class during a meeting he called himself.
jokes.explanation: Michael texting his boss during a call with his boss to arrange a private chat is a perfect encapsulation of his need for special attention and his social obliviousness. The visual of Michael furiously texting under the table is implied and funny. 'I thought maybe we could talk after this is over' as his explanation is beautifully childlike.

jokes.text: After Wallace hangs up, Michael complains: 'You didn't let me say goodbye.'
jokes.setup: The serious Wallace call ends with both managers agreeing to handle it.
jokes.punchline: Michael's only complaint about the difficult business call is that Jim ended it before he could say goodbye.
jokes.explanation: The triviality of Michael's complaint ('you didn't let me say goodbye') against the backdrop of a serious financial decision perfectly captures his emotional priorities. Maximum economy — five words does all the work.

jokes.text: Michael to Jim: 'When I am irritated and I look at you, I don't see you anymore. All I can see is how big and gross the pores on your nose are.'
jokes.setup: Michael says he hates working with Jim and that they work better separately.
jokes.punchline: Michael's expression of frustration escalates from generic dislike to hyper-specific facial critique — he stares at Jim's nose pores when irritated.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'big and gross the pores on your nose are' is excellent. Michael's insult veers from emotional to almost dermatological in a way that's uniquely strange. The setup (general frustration) makes the hyper-specific payoff land better.

jokes.text: Talking head: 'Hey, why haven't we ever, um...' Other person: 'We have.'
jokes.setup: Two employees are in a talking head together. One begins an intimate question.
jokes.punchline: Before the question is finished, the other flatly confirms whatever it was — implying a shared history the first person has forgotten, or the second is bluffing.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully efficient non sequitur talking head. The unfinished question and the immediate confident 'We have' implies an entire relationship history in six words. The comedy is entirely in what's left unsaid. Strong use of the mockumentary format.

jokes.text: Michael's pros and cons list participation: Michael's 'cons' for the equal 1.5% raise include 'you look like a nerd,' 'pro — you get to share your pros and cons list with the other nerds,' and 'con — you unzip your pants, and you find that there's a calculator down there.'
jokes.setup: Jim tries to make a pros and cons list for distributing raises. Michael refuses to engage seriously.
jokes.punchline: Michael's 'contributions' to the list are increasingly absurd personal attacks on Jim for making a list, culminating in the surreal 'calculator in your pants' image.
jokes.explanation: 'You unzip your pants and you find that there's a calculator down there' is an unexpected and funny image for 'you're a nerd.' Michael's total refusal to engage with the list while technically participating in it is a great Michael vs. Jim dynamic. The escalation from 'nerd' insult to surreal pants-calculator is well-paced.

jokes.text: Dwight's talking head with a pie chart: 'I've been studying Michael for years, and I've condensed what I've learned into this chart — how Michael spends his time. As you can see, we have procrastinating and distracting others, and this tiny sliver here is critical thinking. I made it bigger so that you could see it.'
jokes.setup: Dwight presents a pie chart of Michael's time management.
jokes.punchline: The 'critical thinking' slice is so small it had to be artificially enlarged just to be visible — Dwight delivers this as a scientific observation with no trace of irony.
jokes.explanation: The visual gag of the artificially enlarged sliver combined with Dwight's clinical delivery ('I made it bigger so that you could see it') is a perfect Office moment. Dwight's years of studying Michael as a subject is completely in character, and the chart makes his analysis both scientific and devastating. Excellent craft — the visual and verbal elements work together perfectly.

jokes.text: Pam asks for cash as a wedding gift. Kevin: 'Like money? Like you — you want my money?' Pam: 'Mm-hmm.' Kevin: 'Will you take a check?' Pam: 'Yeah.' Kevin: 'Cool. In the memo line, I'm gonna write, "To love's eternal glory."'
jokes.setup: Pam wants cash for a wedding gift instead of registry items.
jokes.punchline: Kevin is genuinely touched by the romance of the transaction — planning to write 'To love's eternal glory' in the memo line of a check for cash, which is the least romantic thing possible.
jokes.explanation: 'To love's eternal glory' on a check is perfectly Kevin — he treats a mercenary cash gift as an opportunity for romantic expression. The deadpan sincerity makes it work. Quotable and endearing.

jokes.text: After discussing Pam's cash gift request, we get Pam's talking head: 'Is this what I've become? Materialistic? Shallow? I feel horrible. Oh, look! "Mrs. Pam Halpert!" That's the first time I've seen it in writing.'
jokes.setup: Pam is having a moment of self-reflection about asking for cash wedding gifts.
jokes.punchline: Her soul-searching is instantly abandoned when she sees her new name in writing — cutting from existential shame to pure joy in one beat.
jokes.explanation: The tonal whiplash is perfectly executed — three lines of sincere self-examination ('materialistic? Shallow? I feel horrible') followed by immediate distraction by something shiny ('Oh, look!'). The emotional beat of seeing 'Mrs. Pam Halpert' for the first time also lands sweetly. The joke and the genuine moment coexist perfectly.

jokes.text: Jim attempts to explain Michael's weaknesses. Michael: 'Why don't you enliven me?' Jim pauses. 'I don't think you're good at making tough decisions.' Michael: 'Okay, here's a tough decision for you. You suck. You suck. Is that clear enough for you?'
jokes.setup: Jim is trying to explain why Michael needs Jim as co-manager — listing Michael's weaknesses diplomatically.
jokes.punchline: Michael asks to be 'enlivened' (meaning enlightened), then responds to Jim's diplomatic critique by making an extremely un-diplomatic decision: just saying 'You suck' twice.
jokes.explanation: 'Why don't you enliven me?' as a malapropism for 'enlighten' is quietly funny. Michael's 'tough decision' demonstration being 'you suck, you suck' proves Jim's entire point about his inability to make tough decisions — while also being very funny. Self-undermining comedy at its best.

jokes.text: Michael: 'I can see it in your crusty little eyes that you are going to make everything perfect... if I can just think this through, if I could just think it exactly right, I can make this perfect... and then another avenue. And then another—'
jokes.setup: Michael is simultaneously criticizing Jim's analytical approach while getting lost in his own spiraling attempt to think through options.
jokes.punchline: Michael's critique of Jim's overthinking becomes a demonstration of Michael's own inability to think — he loses himself in infinite 'avenues' of thought while ostensibly telling Jim not to overthink.
jokes.explanation: Michael criticizing Jim for overthinking while literally spiraling into infinite avenues of thought is a nice structural irony. The escalating self-parody — 'another avenue and then another avenue' — mirrors what he's criticizing. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Michael watches Jim go out to announce the raise decision and mutters under his breath: 'This had better be terrible.'
jokes.setup: Michael just agreed to let Jim make the announcement after telling Jim to 'run himself out there.'
jokes.punchline: Alone in his office, Michael reveals he's actively rooting for Jim to fail — 'This had better be terrible.'
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy and character integration — four words revealing Michael's true relationship to Jim's success. He set Jim up, and now privately hopes he fails. 'This had better be terrible' is one of the episode's most quotable lines. Very Michael.

jokes.text: Jim announces the raise policy honestly. Employee: 'Thank you, Jim, for thinking that we're smart people.' Beat. 'But I do not understand. If we're such smart adults, then why don't we get raises?'
jokes.setup: Jim tells the office the truth about the raises, saying he's 'treating them like adults.'
jokes.punchline: An employee sarcastically thanks Jim for the compliment before pointing out the logical gap: being called smart doesn't offset not getting money.
jokes.explanation: The polite thanks followed by the logical dismantling is a good escalating structure. The setup of Jim's 'treating you like adults' condescension makes the callback sharp. Well-timed.

jokes.text: Dwight in the angry crowd: 'It's because Jim wants to give the raises to his friends and the people he sleeps with.'
jokes.setup: An employee asks why only salespeople get raises if everyone is so smart.
jokes.punchline: Dwight hijacks the legitimate complaint to suggest Jim is engaging in sexual favoritism — framing his personal rivalry as a workplace HR issue.
jokes.explanation: Dwight immediately weaponizing the crowd's anger for his own agenda by implying Jim is sleeping with salespeople is perfectly Dwight. The absurd accusation lands because of the confidence with which it's delivered.

jokes.text: Kelly enters the angry crowd: 'What the hell? Why are you being such a jerk?' Jim: 'Hold on, Kelly.' Kelly: 'Would it help you to know that Jim thinks you're smart?' Kelly: 'No. How is that gonna repair Ryan's car?'
jokes.setup: Kelly joins the angry crowd demanding raises.
jokes.punchline: Jim tries to use his 'I think you're smart' line again. Kelly immediately connects it to Ryan's broken car — a completely unrelated grievance that reveals the size of her personal financial situation.
jokes.explanation: 'How is that gonna repair Ryan's car?' is a perfectly Kelly response — she's immediately connected the raise to a specific, personal, Ryan-related expense. The specificity of 'Ryan's car' is what makes it funny; it's not even her car. Great character integration.

jokes.text: Oscar: 'My kid needs shoes! You want to tell him he doesn't get shoes?' Jim: '...yeah.' Oscar: 'Her kid needs shoes, Jim!'
jokes.setup: The office crowd is escalating its complaints about not getting raises.
jokes.punchline: Oscar claims to have a child who needs shoes — Oscar has no children. Jim's baffled 'yeah' and Oscar's re-emphasis ('Her kid needs shoes, Jim!') pointing to someone else suggests Oscar has just borrowed someone else's kid as rhetorical ammunition.
jokes.explanation: Oscar — the show's most logical, measured character — completely abandoning reason to invoke 'my kid needs shoes' and then immediately revealing it's not his kid ('Her kid needs shoes, Jim!') is exceptional character subversion. The joke works on multiple levels: Oscar joining the mob mentality, the borrowed rhetoric, and Jim's defeated 'yeah.' One of the episode's best laughs.

jokes.text: Jim attempts to regroup: 'Wow. I'm just gonna rewind and back off a bit, so...' Long beat of silence as he retreats.
jokes.setup: Jim has completely lost control of the office crowd.
jokes.punchline: Jim's managerial authority fully collapses — he mimes 'rewinding' and physically retreats. The silence and the camera watching him back away is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The physical retreat and the pause is a good Jim reaction beat — his composure breaking under mob pressure. 'I'm just gonna rewind and back off a bit' is a funny corporate-speak way to say 'I'm fleeing.' Works in context.

jokes.text: Michael enters and attempts to salvage the situation with a speech about the office family: 'They all have heart-ons for you, and that is a gift.' Beat. 'Angela, yes, lend Oscar a cup of sugar. Phyllis, read to Kevin. Andy, tuck Stanley's daughter in bed.'
jokes.setup: Michael sees Jim has failed and tries to give an inspiring speech about workplace community.
jokes.punchline: His speech rapidly devolves into bizarre specific directives — 'lend Oscar a cup of sugar,' 'read to Kevin,' 'tuck Stanley's daughter in bed' — none of which address raises at all.
jokes.explanation: 'Andy, tuck Stanley's daughter in bed' is the highlight — a weirdly specific and inappropriate directive that captures Michael's completely unhinged response to a management crisis. These are non sequiturs masquerading as leadership.

jokes.text: Michael's speech includes: 'They all have heart-ons for you.'
jokes.setup: Michael is giving an inspirational speech about how much the employees care about their managers.
jokes.punchline: Michael uses 'heart-on' as a variant of 'hard-on' — either completely intentionally as a sanitized version or completely unintentionally, which makes it funnier either way. Jim later calls it out.
jokes.explanation: Michael Scott accidentally (or deliberately?) saying 'heart-ons' in a professional address is perfectly in character — he's either sanitizing something inappropriate or is genuinely oblivious. The word is jarring enough that the audience catches it before the characters do, which is great comedy timing. Very quotable and rewatch-worthy because Jim catching it later (joke #62) makes this retroactively funnier.

jokes.text: Meredith speaks up: 'At least Jim was being direct.' Michael: 'Thank you, Meredith.' Meredith: 'When he was telling us his dumbass plan.'
jokes.setup: Michael thanks Meredith for seeming to defend Jim's directness — hearing the first part of her sentence as praise.
jokes.punchline: Meredith completes the sentence with 'when he was telling us his dumbass plan' — she was insulting both of them simultaneously.
jokes.explanation: The structure is clean — Michael mishears praise, thanks Meredith, gets the full sentence in the teeth. 'Dumbass plan' is perfectly Meredith. The two-beat structure (premature thanks, then full context) is a reliable but well-executed structure.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Not to state the obvious, but the only reason I failed out there was because you brought the crowd down.' Jim: 'Okay, you know what? I'm not gonna engage.' Michael: 'They were primed not to like me after you imploded all over them.'
jokes.setup: Michael and Jim retreat to Michael's office after both have failed with the office crowd.
jokes.punchline: Michael reverses causality — claiming Jim 'imploded all over them' first, making them not like Michael, when in fact Michael made things worse. 'Imploded all over them' is also a hilariously wrong use of the word 'imploded.'
jokes.explanation: 'Imploded all over them' is a funny mangled phrase. Michael's complete refusal to accept any responsibility while using completely wrong vocabulary is very in-character.

jokes.text: Michael suggests they 'go in reverse' to erase the bad announcements. 'Close your eyes. Open your eyes. Lollipops and rainbows. Magic words. You're already there.'
jokes.setup: Jim says Michael's speech made things worse. Michael offers a solution.
jokes.punchline: Michael's solution to a management crisis is a visualization exercise involving lollipops, rainbows, and 'magic words' — delivered with the confidence of a life coach.
jokes.explanation: 'Lollipops and rainbows. Magic words. You're already there.' as a crisis management strategy is absurd and very Michael. The delivery matters here — Michael treats this as a real solution.

jokes.text: Jim: 'Do you know you said "heart-on?"'
jokes.setup: Michael has been proudly recounting his speech.
jokes.punchline: Jim finally points out the 'heart-on' slip from earlier — a delayed callback that lands harder because Michael was just defending his speech.
jokes.explanation: The delayed callback works perfectly — waiting to mention it until Michael has been proudly defending his speech makes the deflation better. 'Do you know you said "heart-on?"' is delivered with Jim's classic deadpan and the economy is perfect. Great rewatch value since you're now listening for it in the speech.

jokes.text: Michael and Jim attempt a merit-based raise system using beans placed on photos of employees. Michael: 'Ryan, obviously the best.' Jim: 'Well, obviously. Too bad he's a temp and doesn't count, so let's get started.'
jokes.setup: Michael and Jim are trying to rank employees by merit using a bean-based visual system.
jokes.punchline: Michael's first choice is Ryan, who is a temp and doesn't qualify. The two agree that Ryan is obviously the best employee, which is a joke about their shared delusion and Ryan's strange status in the office.
jokes.explanation: The agreement that Ryan is 'obviously the best' (despite his history on the show as spectacularly bad at his job) is a great in-joke for regular viewers. The bean system itself is a funny premise for a management decision.

jokes.text: Jim defends Pam's position on the raise list. Michael: 'Pam is still lower than Kevin right now.' Jim: 'Kevin sleeps on the toilet.' Michael: 'Still higher than Pam.'
jokes.setup: Jim and Michael are ranking employees by merit. Michael keeps insisting Pam is at the bottom.
jokes.punchline: Jim introduces 'Kevin sleeps on the toilet' as evidence of Kevin's low merit. Michael considers it and still ranks Pam below Kevin — either because he's irrational or because Kevin's toilet napping somehow qualifies as a skill.
jokes.explanation: 'Kevin sleeps on the toilet' / 'Still higher than Pam' is a great exchange — Michael's completely unreasonable stubbornness about Pam's ranking, even in the face of Kevin's toilet habits, is perfectly absurd. The deadpan 'Still higher than Pam' is very funny and very Michael (his long-running dismissal of Pam). Strong economy.

jokes.text: Kevin: 'Oh, I better get that raise. Because once your cats have kittens, all of your priorities change.'
jokes.setup: Employees are venting about needing their raises.
jokes.punchline: Kevin's stated motivation for the raise is that his cats have had kittens — presenting this as a major life event comparable to having children, with the gravity of 'all of your priorities change.'
jokes.explanation: One of the best Kevin lines in the episode. The comedic structure is perfect: a sentence that sounds like it's building to 'I have kids' or a human milestone, but lands on 'cats have kittens.' The earnestness of 'all of your priorities change' maps adult life wisdom onto a pet situation. High quotability and character integration — could only be Kevin.

jokes.text: Various employees in talking heads explaining their need for a raise: 'I need that raise, unless you know a hot tub repair man who will work for empty red wine bottles.'
jokes.setup: Employees explain why they need raises.
jokes.punchline: One employee reveals their hot tub is broken and that their currency situation is: empty red wine bottles. The specificity of the payment method implies a lifestyle that raises questions.
jokes.explanation: 'Empty red wine bottles' as a proposed payment for a hot tub repairman is a beautifully specific detail that paints an entire sad picture of someone's life. The joke works because the specificity implies everything without explaining anything.

jokes.text: Two accounting employees in talking head: 'It's not like we're not gonna see the checks. We're in accounting.' — establishing they can literally see who gets raises.
jokes.setup: Accounting employees complain about not getting raises.
jokes.punchline: They point out their unique torture: being in accounting means they will literally process and see everyone else's larger checks.
jokes.explanation: A smart, specific observational joke about the particular misery of being in accounting during a selective raise season. The logic is airtight and the delivery is understated. Good.

jokes.text: Creed in talking head: 'I am so pissed at this company.' Employee: 'And Jim.' Creed: 'Yeah.' Then: 'Who said that?' Employee: 'I think it was Creed.' Creed: 'Yep.'
jokes.setup: Employees are venting about the raise situation. Someone adds Jim's name to the list of grievances.
jokes.punchline: Creed agrees, then immediately asks who said what he just said, is told it was Creed, and confirms 'Yep' — either he has no short-term memory or he's experiencing a complete dissociative moment.
jokes.explanation: This is quintessential Creed — he immediately forgets that he said something, asks who said it, is told it was him, and accepts this information calmly. The complete loop of 'Creed: [statement] / Creed: Who said that? / Creed: Yep.' is perfectly constructed. Only Creed Bratton could deliver this. High character specificity and quotability. A standout moment for Creed's particular brand of comedy.

jokes.text: Michael and Jim's bean-based merit system: 'Each Boston Baked Bean represents half a percent raise, we each got 24 beans, so the idea is, you place the bean on the picture of who you think deserves...' Michael draws Toby's picture just to exclude him: 'He's not a part of this. You know that.' Michael: 'Just wanted to draw a picture of him.'
jokes.setup: Jim explains the bean-based raise allocation system. Michael includes a picture of Toby.
jokes.punchline: Michael didn't draw Toby to include him — he drew him just to have someone to exclude. Michael's pure petty hatred of Toby motivating even a bureaucratic exercise is perfectly in character.
jokes.explanation: 'Just wanted to draw a picture of him' as Michael's explanation for including Toby only to exclude him is beautifully petty and completely in character. Michael's hatred of Toby is one of the show's running gags, and this is a great specific expression of it. The image of Michael carefully drawing Toby's face just to say he can't participate is funny.

jokes.text: Bean game: Michael announces 'I...will skip a turn.' Jim: 'Okay, you're gonna still have to play that bean. You know that.' Michael: 'I need more time.'
jokes.setup: Michael and Jim are using beans to rank employees for raises. It's Michael's turn.
jokes.punchline: Michael attempts to skip his turn in a bean game — as if the rules of a board game allow passes. Then begs for more time. He is paralyzed by having to make a decision about anyone.
jokes.explanation: Michael's inability to make decisions extended into a literal game — trying to skip a turn, then needing more time. This is a good character beat about Michael's avoidance of difficult choices, previously established in dialogue. The low-stakes absurdity of skipping a bean turn is funny.

jokes.text: Jim reads the email about a Wallace meeting. Long silent pause. Jim stares ahead.
jokes.setup: The raise situation is unresolved. Pam brings news of a meeting with Wallace.
jokes.punchline: Jim's reaction is a prolonged silent stare — the look of a man who has realized co-management with Michael is far worse than he anticipated.
jokes.explanation: A standard Jim camera look stretched into a longer beat. Works as a reaction moment but doesn't reach the level of the best Jim beats in the episode.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head about the raise situation: 'This is worse than I ever possibly could have imagined. And I have imagined some terrible things. Horrible, awful things. Things men do to each other in the heart of battle that the English language doesn't even have words for. Oh. German captures them nicely, but—'
jokes.setup: Michael reacts to the difficulty of the raise situation.
jokes.punchline: Michael escalates from 'worse than I imagined' through increasingly dramatic claims to 'things the English language has no words for' — then the kicker: 'German captures them nicely, but—' implying he regularly thinks in German about war atrocities.
jokes.explanation: The escalating monologue structure is excellent — each sentence raises the stakes of Michael's suffering, building to the absurd claim of war-atrocity-level distress. The final punchline ('German captures them nicely, but—') is the perfect button: it implies Michael knows specific German words for battlefield horrors and regularly references them. The mid-sentence cut makes it funnier. One of the episode's best talking heads.

jokes.text: Creed's wedding gift gambit: 'Would you guys rather have $100 now or $5,000 a year from now?' Pam: '$100 now for sure.' Creed: 'Because you just give me $50 to cover the broker fee, I put in 100 of my own money as the gift...' Pam backs out. Creed: 'Instead of $5,000 a year from now?'
jokes.setup: Creed has heard Pam and Jim want cash as a wedding gift.
jokes.punchline: Creed attempts to run what is clearly a financial scam — offering $5,000 in exchange for $50 upfront 'broker fee' — as a wedding gift. When Pam backs out, Creed plays the offended party.
jokes.explanation: Creed running a scam on the wedding couple as a gift is perfectly, horrifyingly in character. The 'broker fee' framing and his wounded 'Instead of $5,000 a year from now?' when rebuffed shows Creed's complete lack of awareness that he's being a criminal. The algorithm detail ('the guy has an algorithm to determine the winner of any given college basketball game') adds another layer. Very Creed.

jokes.text: Creed adds: 'Don't tell Jim.'
jokes.setup: Creed has just pitched his clearly illegal basketball-algorithm investment scheme to Pam.
jokes.punchline: 'Don't tell Jim' — as if the secrecy instruction makes the scheme more legitimate, or as if Jim's management authority is what makes this inappropriate rather than the fact that it's fraud.
jokes.explanation: 'Don't tell Jim' as a button on an illegal scheme is perfectly Creed — his only concern about the scam is that Jim might find out, not that it's fraud. Maximum economy, perfect character voice.

jokes.text: Office mob storms into Michael's office to see the bean board: 'Come in, feast your eyes. They determine our worth by putting beans upon our faces.'
jokes.setup: The unresolved raise situation has made the office restless. Dwight leads the mob to Michael's office.
jokes.punchline: Dwight announces the bean system to the crowd with theatrical outrage: 'They determine our worth by putting beans upon our faces.' The phrasing ('upon our faces') is archaic and dramatic.
jokes.explanation: 'Beans upon our faces' is Dwight at his most theatrical — using old-fashioned phrasing to make a candy-based administrative exercise sound like an atrocity. Works well as a callback and a Dwight character moment.

jokes.text: Kevin in the mob: 'What does a bean mean?' (asked multiple times)
jokes.setup: The office crowd is angry about the bean-based merit system.
jokes.punchline: Kevin's contribution to the crisis is a repeatedly asked foundational question: 'What does a bean mean?' — suggesting he has missed the entire context of the bean system.
jokes.explanation: 'What does a bean mean?' is perfectly Kevin — a simple question that reveals total incomprehension of the situation. The repetition makes it a running gag and the rhyme ('bean mean') makes it more memorable. Kevin's persistent confusion is a reliable character beat.

jokes.text: Employee to Jim: 'Not according to the beans.' (When Jim says his time is as valuable as Kevin's.)
jokes.setup: Jim says his time is as valuable as Kevin's, frustrated that no one will explain the bean system to Kevin.
jokes.punchline: 'Not according to the beans' — using Jim's own merit-based system against him in a moment of mutiny.
jokes.explanation: 'Not according to the beans' is a sharp, economical line that uses the bean system as a weapon against its creator. The irony of Jim's fair-minded system being immediately used to undermine him is well-structured. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Dwight's speech: 'Are we idiots? An idiot is someone who feels angry and frustrated but instead of doing anything about their problem, they just bang their head into a wall... again and again and again...' [physically bangs head into wall repeatedly]
jokes.setup: Dwight is rallying the office with a rousing anti-Jim speech.
jokes.punchline: To demonstrate what an idiot is NOT, Dwight physically bangs his head into a wall — multiple times — becoming the very thing he's warning against.
jokes.explanation: Great escalating physical comedy. Dwight's definition of an idiot involves head-banging into a wall — which he demonstrates with increasing conviction — until he's doing exactly what he's warning against. The 'Are you okay?' / 'I'm fine.' button is a perfect deadpan capper. Strong character integration — Dwight's all-in commitment to physical demonstration is very him.

jokes.text: Dwight's motivational speech to the office mob: 'What right does Jim have to claim authority, hmm? Think about it. Is he as good a salesman as I? Is he as smart as Oscar? Is he as matronly as Phyllis? Some rule by imposing their rule through their heft. Is he heftier than—' Oscar: 'We get it.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is trying to rouse the office to rebel against Jim.
jokes.punchline: Dwight's revolutionary speech pivots from intelligence and sales ability to 'matronly' (as a positive quality?) and then is building to 'heft' as a management criterion when Oscar simply cuts him off: 'We get it.'
jokes.explanation: 'Is he as matronly as Phyllis?' is the episode's funniest Dwight moment in this sequence — using 'matronly' as a positive leadership quality while Phyllis is in the room is wonderfully specific and bizarre. Oscar's 'We get it' cutting off the 'heft' comparison is a perfect reaction. Dwight's earnest revolutionary rhetoric is very in-character.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'Is he as matronly as Phyllis?'
jokes.setup: Dwight is making the case that Jim has no special authority.
jokes.punchline: Dwight lists Phyllis's 'matronliness' as a genuine professional qualification — implying being matronly is a standard by which managers should be judged.
jokes.explanation: 'Is he as matronly as Phyllis?' is a funny line because 'matronly' is delivered as a legitimate professional credential. Dwight's odd criteria for management quality — including matronliness — is absurd and specific.

jokes.text: Dwight's full revolutionary speech: 'For a few seconds every decade, we exist, and these are those seconds. Let us storm his castle. Come on. Tick — let's get him. Tock — let's get Jim! Tick — and drag Jim out of his office. Tock — take his keys away from him. Tick — that's a clock. The time is getting very close.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is building to a rousing call to revolt against Jim.
jokes.punchline: The speech escalates from genuine revolutionary rhetoric to Dwight explaining that tick-tock is a clock — undermining his own dramatic momentum by feeling the need to clarify a basic metaphor. The mob's non-response follows.
jokes.explanation: 'Tick — that's a clock' mid-revolutionary-speech is Dwight's self-undermining at its finest — he loses confidence in his metaphor and has to explain it. The speech is building well and then deflates itself. Very in-character for Dwight's mix of grandiosity and insecurity.

jokes.text: Dwight's rally ends: 'What say you?' Office worker: 'I say no.' Dwight: 'No, I mean, what do you say to my plan?' Office: [silence/no]
jokes.setup: Dwight asks the mob if they're ready to revolt.
jokes.punchline: One person simply says 'I say no' — Dwight clarifies he meant the plan, and the answer is still no. The revolutionary speech has moved nobody.
jokes.explanation: The deflation of Dwight's speech by a single 'I say no' is a good button. The misunderstanding (answering for themselves rather than the plan) adds a layer. The mob's unanimously unenthusiastic response to Dwight's revolution is perfectly sad.

jokes.text: 'What does a bean mean?' — Kevin, one final time, after everything has collapsed.
jokes.setup: The entire office revolt has fizzled. Everyone is standing around in deflated confusion.
jokes.punchline: Kevin asks the same question one more time — his persistence in not understanding anything is the final word on the office's competence.
jokes.explanation: The final 'What does a bean mean?' lands harder than the earlier repetitions because the question now has maximum irony — the entire crisis has resolved (sort of) and Kevin still hasn't grasped the basic premise. It's a perfect coda to the chaos. The repetition structure makes this callback stronger than any individual instance.

jokes.text: Jim and Michael sit together in defeat. Jim: 'On a scale of one to ten, I'd say I'm about a four.' Michael: 'Oh, what are you usually?' Jim: 'Six. You?' Michael: 'Usually a ten, but I'm feeling like a zero.'
jokes.setup: Jim and Michael are sitting together having both failed to manage the raise situation.
jokes.punchline: Michael's self-assessment that he's 'usually a ten' — said with complete sincerity — is the joke. The contrast between his self-perception and reality is the entire Michael Scott character in one exchange.
jokes.explanation: Michael's certainty that he's 'usually a ten' is quietly devastating. The exchange also has a genuine melancholy that makes it more than just a joke — both men have had a terrible day, and Michael's delusion is both funny and sad. Good character moment.

jokes.text: Michael's scale of 1-10: Jim says he's 'about a four.' Michael says he's 'usually a ten, but feeling like a zero.' Jim: 'Oh, what are you usually?' Michael: 'Usually a ten.'
jokes.setup: Jim and Michael are sharing how they're feeling after a terrible day.
jokes.punchline: Michael's self-assessment is 'usually a ten' — maximum confidence — dropping to a zero today. The combination of habitual 10/10 self-rating and current 0/10 is a good Michael encapsulation.
jokes.explanation: Michael self-rating as a habitual 10 is consistent and funny. The dramatic collapse to zero and back to '...usually a ten' when Jim asks for clarification is a small but good character beat.

jokes.text: Michael (genuinely, quietly): 'I used to have to do this part alone, and it was the worst.' He gives Jim a bottle of gin.
jokes.setup: Jim and Michael have both failed and are sitting in defeat.
jokes.punchline: Michael's moment of genuine emotional connection — acknowledging he used to face bad management days alone — is expressed by giving Jim a bottle of gin. The gin is the joke; the sentiment is real.
jokes.explanation: The gin gift is funny because it's Michael's version of emotional support — sharing a bottle of gin with a subordinate. But the moment also has genuine warmth. This is the Office at its best: comedy and heart simultaneously. The 'What's in here?' / 'Gin.' exchange is perfectly deadpan.

jokes.text: Michael: 'I used to have to do this part alone, and it was the worst.'
jokes.setup: Michael and Jim are commiserating after a terrible day managing together.
jokes.punchline: Michael's admission that he actually appreciates having Jim around — framed not as warmth but as a relief from loneliness — is both genuinely touching and unintentionally funny.
jokes.explanation: A quietly sweet and funny moment. Michael's begrudging appreciation for company is perfectly in character. The line works emotionally and comedically — the show is at its best when Michael's pathos and humor are the same thing.

jokes.text: Michael, Jim, and Pam drink gin in the office while the angry staff presses against the glass. Michael: 'Just pretend we're not here.' Jim: 'Okay.'
jokes.setup: The office staff is still angry about raises. Michael, Jim, and Pam are hiding in Michael's office drinking gin.
jokes.punchline: 'Just pretend we're not here' — said by the people who are clearly visible through a glass office wall, drinking during working hours.
jokes.explanation: The visual of three managers hiding and drinking in a glass office while employees watch is inherently funny. Michael's 'Just pretend we're not here' followed by Jim's cooperative 'Okay' suggests they both know this is absurd. A strong visual gag that captures the episode's collapse of authority.

jokes.text: Final Dwight talking head: 'So it appears I acted too soon. I'm not worried. I'll get Jim yet. All I need is a plan, a devious plan. No. A diabolical plan.'
jokes.setup: The episode ends with Dwight reflecting on the failed revolt.
jokes.punchline: Dwight self-corrects from 'devious' to 'diabolical' — spending his cognitive energy on adjective selection rather than actual planning. The upgrade implies 'diabolical' is more threatening, which it isn't really.
jokes.explanation: A perfect button for the episode. Dwight has failed completely but is already re-planning with upgraded vocabulary. The self-correction from 'devious' to 'diabolical' is a small but effective character beat — Dwight's theatrical self-seriousness persists through total defeat. Good closing joke.

tmdb_overview: David Wallace comes bearing the news that not all the staffers will receive a raise this year. Jim pushes Dwight to the limit and causes him to form office alliances. And Pam decides she wants only cash as a wedding gift.
